project1.title: The SUPER Assessor
project1.summary: Developed as a part of the full-stack web development course in 2024, the project was developed with 2 students from BWU. The application helps teachers create and evaluate assessment forms using a card-based game. Application is built using the MERN stack.

project2.title: Travel Website with a Focus on Accessibility
project2.summary: For the course accessibility, usability, and ethics course, I built a travel-themed website that focuses on accessible and inclusive design. The goal was to build a website that users with various disabilities could navigate and interact with easily, following the WCAG guidelines (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines).

project3.title: E-Learning Platform for the Shared Model
project3.summary: For the bachelor's project we developed an e-learning platform for the Shared Model. Me and 2 other students worked in collaboration with Helseinn and Helsefelleskapet Innlandet. The goal was to make training in the shared model in the healthcare and municipal sector more accessible and effective through user-friendly design, interactive modules, and research-based content.

header1.title: Introduction
header1.p1: At the beginning of the project, we were tasked with creating a digital version of SUPER Assessor, a card game developed at NTNU to help educators design new forms of assessment. Here you can see the physical version of the game
header1.p2: The goal was to use Web Components to build reusable card components with support for data transfer, styling via custom properties, and interaction using Custom Events. The first part focused on learning React and APIs, while the final assignment, where we built a full-stack application using MongoDB, Express JS, React, and Node JS (MERN), was done in groups. We also got access to design files and an Excel sheet containing card data that we could use in the project. The main project was developed in collaboration with two other NTNU students.
header1.p3: I started by setting up the structure of the project and experimenting with how HTML attributes and JS properties could be used to dynamically generate the cards. I used the design files and data from the Excel sheet to create a component structure that could display and handle interactive cards, including bookmarking and flip functionality.
header1.p4: Here is an image of the database we used to dynamically generate the cards. There were a total of 86 cards in the database.

header2.title: Implementation and design
header2.p1: The full-stack project was built on previous mandatory assignments we had throughout the semester. The first part with Web Components and API solutions formed the foundation, and we had the opportunity to reuse and improve much of the code we had already created. To plan how we would develop a complete solution as a group, we created Figma prototypes and discussed user flow, component structure, and design choices. This gave us a clear direction before moving on with the implementation.

header3.title: Final results
header3.p1: In the final part of the project, we focused on further developing and completing a full version of SUPER Assessor v2.0 as a full-stack application. This was not only about implementing the final requirements, but also about ensuring that earlier functionality was stable, secure, and well-documented.
list: Authentication for different user types (teacher, admin, and visitor).
Game flow where teachers can draw cards from different decks and build assessment schemes.
Ability to save, evaluate, and share assessment schemes.
PDF generation with front and back of cards, adjusted to card size and ready for print.
An extended favorites feature using localStorage for bookmarking. An improved user experience and responsive design.
header3.p2: We also emphasized backend functionality, including a well-structured REST API, security measures, and documentation via Swagger. For the frontend, we mainly used React but had requirements to reuse Web Components from earlier assignments now improved in structure and flexibility. The project was finalized with testing and quality assurance to ensure that all roles (visitor, teacher, and admin) could perform their tasks without errors. We worked closely as a team and clearly distributed responsibilities something that contributed to a successful delivery and better understanding of how to build modern web applications in practice.

header1.title: Introduction
header1.p1: The goal of this project was to develop an accessible and responsive travel website for people aged 18–35. The focus was on universal design and a good user experience for everyone, regardless of functional ability. I began by analyzing user needs and conducted a small survey with people who use screen readers.

header2.title: Design and development
header2.p1: To ensure accessibility and usability, I started by designing a simple and structured layout in Figma. I followed the WCAG guidelines and conducted early testing using various assistive technologies such as screen readers and keyboard navigation.
header2.p2: I emphasized semantic HTML, clear ARIA labels, a skip-to-main function, and high contrast. The layout was intentionally simple and consistent across pages to make navigation intuitive. In addition, media queries and relative units were used to ensure good responsiveness.

header3.title: Testing and results
header3.p1: The focus was on testing the website and improving the accessibility. I used tools like the WAVE evaluation tool and WebAIM Contrast Checker for color contrast, and tested with screen readers like Windows Narrator and ChromeVox. Feedback from fellow students led to improvements in focus handling and link descriptions.
header3.p2: A concrete example was changing unclear links like "Click here" to more descriptive alternatives such as "Read about Paris." I also added more semantic HTML elements and ARIA attributes to enhance the screen reader experience.
list: Closed captions and transcripts for media
Responsive design on all screen sizes

header1.title: Introduction
header1.p1: The bachelor's project began in 2024 as part of the course In-depth project. We worked together with Helseinn for the project 'Felles modell for tjenesteutvikling i Helsefellesskap Innlandet'. Me and two other students started working on the insight and research part through a competitor analysis of existing e-learning platforms.
header1.p2: The project was started to make training in the Shared Model more accessible for employees in healthcare and municipal sectors in the Innlandet region. We conducted interviews with the target group to learn about the challenges they face when using e-learning platforms. The aim was to understand how an e-learning course could improve understanding and the implementation of the Shared Model in practice.
header1.p3: We looked at literature and theories related to the pedagogical part of learning and motivation and based on this, we defined clear goals for the e-learning course, with a focus on usability, adaptability, effective learning, and user-friendliness.

header2.title: Design and development
header2.p1: After conducting interviews and a literature review, we started prototyping the e-learning course. We used Figma to create a prototype of the course, which was then tested with users. The feedback was used to improve the design and functionality of the course.
header2.p3: In addition to the e-learning course, which was our main focus, the project owner asked us to create a form for creating reports for the Shared Model. Each step of the Shared Model has reports that has to be sent to Strategic Collaboration Comittee (SSU) we completed the e-learning course first and made, before we created the forms.
header2.p4: Screenshot of the landing page that greets users when they first access the Shared Model's page.

header3.title: Final results
header3.p1: The project is complete, the Shared Model learning platform has finished development, but the e-learning modules are still under development. We have finish creating the first e-learning module and conducted user testing of the Shared Model learning platform with the target group. The testing has given us valuable insight into how users understand the content, navigate the platform, and experience the course structure. Based on the user testing we have fixed numerous issues.
header3.p2: The feedback has been used to improve the e-learning modules. We are documenting the process in our bachelor thesis report. The final project deadline was May 15, 2025.
